problem:
Iodine-131 has a half-life of $8.02$ days. A sample of iodine-131 has an initial mass of $7.2\,\mu \text{g}.$ Rounded to **one decimal place**, what is the mass of the sample after $12$ days?

The mass of the sample after $12$ days is approximately
{{field-1}}
$\mu \text{g}.$

activity_context.topic_title: Exponential Growth and Decay Models With First-Order ODEs: Half-Life Problems

feedback.problem: The half-life of astatine-223 is $50\,\text{s}.$ How long does it take for an $400\,\mu \text{g}$ sample of astatine-223 to reduce to $50\,\mu \text{g}?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The mass $M(t)$ of a radioactive substance at time $t$ can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
{M}^{′}(t)=-kM(t),\,M(0)={M}_{0}.
$$

The general solution to this equation is

$$
M(t)={M}_{0}{e}^{-kt}.
$$

The half-life ${t}_{1/2}$ is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

$$
{t}_{1/2}=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}.
$$

There are two methods that we can use to solve this problem. We describe each of them below.

**Method 1**

Since we know that ${t}_{1/2}=50\,\text{s},$ we have

$$
50=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}\,⇒\,k=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{50}
$$

Also, since ${M}_{0}=400\,\mu \text{g},$ we have the particular solution

$$
M(t)=400{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/50}.
$$

We wish to calculate the time $t$ such that $M(t)=50\,\mu \text{g}.$ So, we set up our equation as follows:

$$
50=400{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/50}\,\,
$$

Solving this equation for $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}50 & =400{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/50} \\ \frac{50}{400} & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/50} \\ \frac{1}{8} & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/50} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{8}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/50}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡8 & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{50} \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡8 & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{50} \\ t & =\frac{50\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡8}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ t & =150.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that it takes $150\,\text{s}$ for the mass of the substance to reduce to $50\,\mu \text{g}.$

**Method 2**

We wish to calculate the time $t$ such that $M(t)=50\,\mu \text{g}.$ Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{M(t)}{M(0)} & =\frac{50\,\mu \text{g}}{400\,\mu \text{g}} \\  & =\frac{1}{8} \\  & ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{3},\end{aligned}
$$

or equivalently

$$
M(t)={(\frac{1}{2})}^{3}\cdot M(0).
$$

From this equation, we see that $3$ half-lives must have occurred for the mass to reduce from $400\,\mu \text{g}$ to $50\,\mu \text{g}.$ Hence,

$$
t=3\cdot {t}_{1/2}=3\cdot 50\,\text{s}=150\,\text{s}.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that it takes $150\,\text{s}$ for the mass of the substance to reduce to $50\,\mu \text{g}.$
